DataScience X Logistic Regression (DSLR) is a 42 Machine Learning branch project in which you write a one-vs-all logistic regression classifier that sorts Hogwarts students into the four houses and rebuilds the bewitched Sorting Hat.

DataScience X Logistic Regression (DSLR), also called "Harry Potter and a Data Scientist", is a 42 Machine Learning branch assignment: the Sorting Hat of Hogwarts has been bewitched and can no longer sort students, so Professor McGonagall asks a muggle data scientist to rebuild it. The student reads and cleans a dataset of Hogwarts students, explores it through statistics and plots, then trains a one-vs-all logistic regression classifier that predicts each student's house with at least 98% accuracy.

The Data Analysis part (V.1) requires a program describe.[extension] that takes a CSV dataset and prints, for every numerical feature, the Count, Mean, Std, Min, 25%, 50%, 75% and Max, reimplemented from scratch. Using count, mean, std, min, max, percentile or any pandas-describe-like helper is considered cheating, in any language.

The Data Visualization part (V.2) asks for three scripts, each answering a question with a plot: histogram.[extension] finds which Hogwarts course has a homogeneous score distribution across the four houses; scatter_plot.[extension] finds the two features that are similar; pair_plot.[extension] draws a scatter-plot matrix used to decide which features feed the logistic regression.

The Logistic Regression part (V.3) is a one-vs-all multi-classifier made of two programs. logreg_train.[extension] takes dataset_train.csv, minimizes the error with gradient descent and writes a weights file. logreg_predict.[extension] takes dataset_test.csv plus that weights file and outputs houses.csv, formatted with an "Index,Hogwarts House" header and one predicted house (Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, Slytherin) per row.

During peer-evaluation the work is judged on the Git turn-in and on the student's ability to present, explain and justify the machine-learning choices; the classifier is scored with Scikit-Learn's accuracy on dataset_test.csv and must reach 98% precision. The bonus part (extra describe fields, stochastic gradient descent, batch / mini-batch GD, other optimizers) is only assessed if the mandatory part is perfect. The math annex gives the logistic cost function J(theta) (log-loss / cross-entropy), the hypothesis h(x) = g(theta^T x), the sigmoid g(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z) and the partial derivative used by gradient descent.

Multilayer Perceptron is a 42 Machine Learning project that introduces artificial neural networks by having you implement, from scratch, a multilayer perceptron that predicts whether a breast tumour is malignant or benign from the Wisconsin diagnostic dataset.

The Multilayer Perceptron project is an introduction to artificial neural networks: in the language of your choice you implement a feedforward multilayer perceptron from scratch (no neural-network libraries, though linear-algebra and plotting libraries are allowed) to classify breast-cancer diagnoses as malignant or benign. A Makefile is required for compiled languages, the project is evaluated only by humans, and part of the grade depends on explaining feedforward, backpropagation and gradient descent.

The introduction covers the history and theory: Turing's 1948 B-type unorganised machine, Rosenblatt's 1957 single-layer perceptron, and the later multilayer perceptron. A multilayer perceptron is a feedforward network with one or more fully-connected (dense) hidden layers, weight matrices W between layers and a bias neuron whose output is always 1. A single perceptron computes a weighted sum of the previous layer's outputs plus a bias, then applies an activation function such as sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent or rectified linear unit (ReLU).

The dataset is a CSV with 32 columns; the diagnosis column is the label to predict (M for malignant or B for benign) and the other features describe a cell nucleus of a breast mass obtained by fine-needle aspiration. There is an important data-understanding and preprocessing phase (explore, plot, visualize the features), and the student must split the raw data into a training set and a validation set.

The implementation must contain at least two hidden layers by default and be modular, configured through a file or CLI arguments (for example --layer 24 24 24 --epochs 84 --loss categoricalCrossentropy --batch_size 8 --learning_rate 0.0314), with a softmax output layer producing a probability distribution, a weights initializer such as heUniform, and two learning-curve graphs (loss and accuracy) displayed at the end of training.

Three programs are submitted (or one program with a mode switch): a split program (a seed is allowed for reproducibility), a training program that learns with backpropagation and gradient descent and saves the model topology and weights, and a prediction program that loads those weights, predicts on a set and evaluates it with the binary cross-entropy error function. Training and validation metrics (loss, val_loss) are displayed at each epoch.

The bonus part is graded only if the mandatory part is perfect and includes a more complex optimizer (Nesterov momentum, RMSprop, Adam...), several learning curves on one graph to compare models, a history of training metrics, early stopping, and evaluation with multiple metrics.

Total Perspective Vortex is a 42 Machine Learning project in which you build a brain-computer interface that uses machine learning on EEG data to infer, in near real time, which movement a subject performs or imagines.

Total Perspective Vortex ("Plug your brain to the shell") asks you to create a brain-computer interface from electroencephalographic (EEG) data with machine-learning algorithms. Using a subject's EEG reading from a motor-imagery experiment (doing or imagining a hand or feet movement shown as an on-screen symbol), you infer motion A or B over a t0..tn timeframe. You must code in Python because it provides MNE (EEG processing) and scikit-learn (machine learning), and you implement a dimensionality-reduction algorithm integrated into sklearn.

The goals are: process EEG data (parsing and filtering), implement a dimensionality-reduction algorithm, use the scikit-learn Pipeline object, and classify a data stream in "real time". The preprocessing step parses and explores EEG data with MNE from PhysioNet, visualizes the raw signal, filters it to keep only useful frequency bands, and visualizes again; this is where you decide which features to extract (for example the signal power by frequency and by channel). Filtering and spectrum estimation typically use the Fourier transform or the wavelet transform (bonus).

The treatment pipeline chains a dimensionality-reduction algorithm (PCA, ICA, CSP, CSSP...), a classification algorithm from sklearn, and a "playback" reading of the file to simulate a data stream. It is advised to first test the architecture with sklearn/MNE algorithms before implementing your own CSP. The program has a training script and a prediction script; the prediction must run on a stream and output before a 2-second delay after each chunk is sent (mne-realtime is not allowed), and you must use the sklearn Pipeline with the BaseEstimator and TransformerMixin classes.

The implementation focuses on the dimensionality-reduction algorithm: express the data with the most meaningful features by determining a projection matrix that performs a change of basis (rotations, translations, scaling). PCA finds new basis components sorted by how much variance they explain; CSP (common spatial patterns) analyses the data by output class and maximizes the variance between classes, and is more common in EEG BCIs. The objective is to find a transformation matrix W such that W^T X = X_CSP; NumPy or SciPy functions for eigenvalues, singular values and covariance-matrix estimation are allowed.

For train, validation and test you must use cross_val_score on the whole processing pipeline, choose your own split between Train, Validation and Test sets (without overfitting, using different splits each time), and reach at least 60% mean accuracy on all test subjects across the six experiment run types on never-seen data. You may train and predict on the subject and task of your choice; example commands are `python mybci.py 4 14 train` and `python mybci.py 4 14 predict`. Bonuses include wavelet-transform preprocessing, implementing your own classifier or another pipeline step, working on other datasets, and coding your own eigenvalue / SVD / covariance functions. The foreword quotes Douglas Adams' Total Perspective Vortex from The Restaurant at the End of the Universe.

Learn2Slither is a 42 artificial-intelligence project about reinforcement learning: a snake moving on a 10x10 board is controlled by a Q-learning agent that learns by trial and error to survive and grow to a length of 10 or more.

Learn2Slither is a reinforcement-learning project where you build a snake on a board controlled by an intelligent agent. Reinforcement learning lets machines learn by trial and error, refining behaviour from feedback in the form of rewards or punishments. Each choice the agent makes gets positive or negative feedback from the board, and the agent adapts to maximize rewards over time. Python is recommended (respecting the flake8 norm), and the board, the agent and the trained models are submitted to git.

The environment is a 10x10 board with two green apples and one red apple at random cells. The snake starts at length 3, placed randomly and contiguously. Hitting a wall, colliding with its own tail, or dropping to length 0 ends the training session. Eating a green apple grows the snake by 1 (and spawns a new green apple); eating a red apple shrinks it by 1. Training needs hundreds or thousands of sessions, set by a command-line parameter, and a graphical interface must display the board over time with a configurable speed, at least one human-readable speed and a step-by-step mode.

The state is the snake's vision: it can only see in the 4 directions from its head. The program prints a terminal view using W = wall, H = snake head, S = snake body segment, G = green apple, R = red apple and 0 = empty space. Giving the agent any information beyond this vision results in a -42 penalty. The agent can perform only 4 actions (UP, LEFT, DOWN, RIGHT) and must decide solely from the snake vision.

Rewards are defined by the student: an obvious scheme gives a negative reward for eating a red apple, a positive reward for a green apple, a smaller negative reward for eating nothing, and a bigger negative reward for game over. Each reward raises or lowers the chance the agent repeats the same choice in an identical situation. The goal is to reach a length of at least 10 and stay alive as long as possible.

The learning model must use a Q function to evaluate the quality of an action in a state, implemented with Q-values in a Q-table or a neural network; no other model is allowed (otherwise a score of 0). The Q function is updated from the reward after each action, with exploration versus exploitation (sometimes taking random actions) and iterative learning across sessions. A single model file (mostly Q-values) can be exported and re-imported, and an "exploitation without learning" switch lets you evaluate a model without altering it; the display and terminal output can be disabled to speed up training.

For turn-in the program must be modular, with a "models" folder containing trained models in a file format of your choice. You must provide at least 3 saved models trained with 1, 10 and 100 sessions to show how the snake learns, and be able to start a new session from a saved model with the non-learning feature to verify its performance. Example command lines are `./snake -sessions 10 -save models/10sess.txt -visual off` and `./snake -visual on -load models/100sess.txt -sessions 10 -dontlearn -step-by-step`. Bonuses (only if all mandatory parts are correct) include reaching higher lengths (15 to 35), a visually stunning display with lobby and statistics, and a configurable board size that works with the same trained models. Machine Learning Module 00 ("Stepping into Machine Learning") is the first module of the 42AI Python & Machine Learning bootcamp: you review linear algebra and statistics, implement a first linear model and learn to evaluate its performance with loss functions.

Module 00 reviews the maths you need (sum, mean, variance, standard deviation, vector and matrix operations) and the core notions of hypothesis, model, regression and loss function, following the Stanford Machine Learning MOOC. Common instructions: Python 3.7, PEP 8 / pycodestyle, the eval function is never allowed, exercises go from easiest to hardest, and work is submitted to a git repository graded by peers and Deepthought.

Exercise 00, TinyStatistician, is a class with mean, median (the 50th percentile), quartile (25th and 75th percentiles), percentile(x, p), var (sample variance) and std (sample standard deviation), all implemented from scratch without any library statistics function, protecting against bad input by returning None and never raising an exception; it also clarifies the population versus sample definitions.

Exercises 01 and 02 introduce the linear-algebra trick: add_intercept adds a column of ones to x to form the X' matrix so the hypothesis becomes y_hat = X' . theta = theta0 + theta1 x, and predict_ computes the whole prediction vector in one matrix multiplication. The theta notation replaces a and b, and the task is regression: predicting a continuous numerical value such as a price.

Exercises 03 to 06 cover plotting and loss: plot draws the data points and the prediction (regression) line from x, y and theta, and plot_with_loss also shows the overall loss J in the title and draws the distance lines between points and predictions. The loss function J(theta) = 1/(2m) sum (y_hat - y)^2 (half mean squared error), also written vectorized as 1/(2m)(y_hat - y).(y_hat - y); exercise 05 adds MSE, RMSE, MAE and the R2 score, cross-checked against sklearn.metrics.

Exercise 07, The Matrix, has you build Matrix and Vector classes without NumPy: data as a list of lists plus a shape tuple, the magic methods __add__, __sub__, __truediv__, __mul__ (scalars, vectors and matrices), __str__ and __repr__, and a .T() transpose method; Vector inherits from Matrix, checks it is a row or column vector, and has a .dot() method. The conclusion asks you to explain the column of ones, why the loss squares the distances, what the loss represents, and why matrix multiplication is not commutative.

Machine Learning Module 01 ("Univariate Linear Regression") teaches gradient descent to train a one-variable linear regression model and introduces feature normalization.

Module 01 builds on module 00's predict-evaluate-improve cycle and tackles the "improve" step: its notions are gradient descent, linear regression and normalization, following the Stanford MOOC sections on gradient descent and feature scaling.

Exercise 00 shows that improving a model means reducing the loss J: plotting J against theta1 gives a convex curve whose minimum we seek, and the slope (derivative) tells which way to move. Because there are two parameters, J has two partial derivatives packaged into the gradient vector, computed vectorized as grad(J) = 1/m X'^T (X' theta - y), where X'^T is the transpose of the design matrix with a column of ones added.

Exercise 01 implements gradient descent itself: for max_iter iterations, compute grad(J) then update theta := theta - alpha grad(J). Alpha is the learning rate, a small float usually between 0 and 1, so the steps do not overshoot the minimum; too large an alpha makes theta become nan, and alpha and the number of cycles are chosen by trial and error. The fit_ function returns the new theta.

Exercises 02 and 03 build a MyLinearRegression class mirroring sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression with fit_, predict_, loss_elem_ and loss_ methods, then practice on are_blue_pills_magics.csv (space pilots' driving score versus the dose of "blue pills" taken): read the CSV, run a linear regression, plot the data with the hypothesis and the loss curve J(theta), and compute the MSE. Scikit-learn is only for cross-checking and is forbidden in the turn-in.

Exercises 04 and 05 cover normalization: z-score standardization x' = (x - mu) / sigma maps values to roughly [-1, 1], and min-max standardization x' = (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x)) maps them to [0, 1]. Scaling the data speeds up (or even enables) gradient-descent convergence when feature magnitudes vary a lot. The conclusion asks you to explain the hypothesis, the loss function, linear gradient descent, what happens with a learning rate that is too large or too small, and what MSE measures.

Machine Learning Module 02 ("Multivariate Linear Regression") extends linear regression to several features, builds polynomial models, and teaches how to detect overfitting by splitting data into training and test sets.

Module 02's notions are the multivariate linear hypothesis, multivariate gradient descent, polynomial models, training and test sets, and overfitting, following the Stanford MOOC Week 2 (multiple features, gradient descent for multiple variables, feature scaling, learning rate, polynomial regression).

Exercises 00 and 01 handle multivariate prediction: training examples become an (m x n) design matrix X, the hypothesis is y_hat(i) = theta0 + theta1 x1(i) + ... + thetan xn(i), a column of ones added to X gives X' so y_hat = X' . theta, and the loss function is unchanged from module 00 because it only uses y_hat and y.

Exercises 02 to 04 cover the multivariate gradient and gradient descent: the gradient now has n+1 components, grad(J) = 1/m X'^T (X' theta - y), and descent updates theta := theta - alpha grad(J) for j from 0 to n; we subtract because the gradient points uphill and we want to minimize. The MyLinearRegression class from module 01 is upgraded (predict_, fit_) to support multivariate hypotheses.

Exercise 05 practices on spacecraft_data.csv (Sell_price plus Age, Thrust_power and Terameters): part one trains three separate univariate models, one per feature, and plots predictions against actual prices; part two trains a single multivariate model on all three features, interprets the theta parameters, and compares the MSE. If theta becomes nan, reduce the learning rate.

Exercises 06 and 07 introduce polynomial models: add_polynomial_features raises x to powers 2, 3, 4... building a Vandermonde matrix x | x^2 | ... | x^n, and the polynomial hypothesis y_hat = theta0 + theta1 x + theta2 x^2 + ... introduces non-linearity. Six models of degree 1 to 6 are trained on are_blue_pills_magics, with an MSE bar plot and the six curves plotted; smooth curves need many points.

Exercises 08 and 09 are about overfitting and data splitting: a high polynomial degree increases complexity and causes overfitting (the model fits noise and fails to generalize), so you must always evaluate on unseen data. data_spliter shuffles and splits x and y into a training and a test set by a given proportion (a seed makes it reproducible). Machine Learning Module 03 ("Logistic Regression") introduces the first classification algorithm, with the sigmoid hypothesis, the cross-entropy loss, logistic gradient descent, one-vs-all multiclass classification and evaluation metrics.

Module 03's notions are the logistic hypothesis, logistic gradient descent, logistic regression, multiclass classification, and the metrics accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score and confusion matrix, following the Stanford MOOC Week 3 (classification, hypothesis representation, decision boundary, cost function, one-vs-all).

Exercises 00 and 01 build the hypothesis: classification predicts categories or labels rather than numbers, classes are coded 0 and 1, and the sigmoid function sigmoid(x) = 1 / (1 + e^-x) squashes any real number to a probability in [0, 1]. The logistic hypothesis y_hat = sigmoid(theta . x') = 1 / (1 + e^-(X' theta)) is simply the sigmoid applied on top of the linear regression hypothesis, and its output is read as the probability of belonging to a class.

Exercise 02 derives the cross-entropy loss: the squared-distance loss is inappropriate for classification, so a logarithmic loss is used, with lossy=1 = -log(y_hat) and lossy=0 = -log(1 - y_hat) combined using y itself as a switch, giving J(theta) = -1/m sum [y log(y_hat) + (1 - y) log(1 - y_hat)]. It is vectorized with a vector of ones, an epsilon avoids log(0), and NumPy broadcasting is a common source of bugs.

Exercises 03 and 04 cover the logistic gradient and class: the gradient formula grad(J) = 1/m X'^T (h_theta(X) - y) is the same as in linear regression, only the hypothesis changes to the sigmoid. The MyLogisticRegression class (predict_, loss_elem_, loss_, fit_) is a simplified version of sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression.

Exercise 05 practices on the solar_system_census dataset (height, weight, bone density plus a planet zipcode: 0 the flying cities of Venus, 1 United Nations of Earth, 2 Mars Republic, 3 the Asteroids' Belt colonies). mono_log.py takes --zipcode=x, relabels each citizen 1 or 0, trains a binary classifier, reports the fraction of correct predictions on the test set and plots 3 scatter plots. multi_log.py applies one-versus-all: it trains 4 logistic classifiers and, for each example, picks the class with the highest output probability.

Exercises 06 and 07 add evaluation metrics: the two error types are false positives (a non-A object assigned to class A) and false negatives (an A object assigned elsewhere). accuracy = (tp + tn) / total, precision = tp / (tp + fp) (controls false positives), recall = tp / (tp + fn) (controls false negatives) and F1 score = 2 . precision . recall / (precision + recall). You reimplement these sklearn.metrics functions and the confusion_matrix (true labels as rows, predicted as columns), with an optional pandas DataFrame version. The conclusion asks why a logistic rather than linear hypothesis is used, what the decision boundary is, how many regressors are needed for N classes, the difference between accuracy and precision, type I and type II errors, and the interest of the F1 score.

Machine Learning Module 04 ("Regularization") teaches how to fight overfitting with L2 regularization, applied to the loss functions and gradients of linear and logistic regression, leading to Ridge regression and regularized logistic regression.

Module 04's notions are regularization, overfitting, the regularized loss function, regularized gradient descent, regularized linear regression (Ridge) and regularized logistic regression, following the Stanford MOOC Week 3.
Exercise 00 extends add_polynomial_features to a matrix X of shape (m x n), raising every column to the powers 1 to p and returning a matrix of shape (m x (n*p)).

Exercise 01 introduces the L2 regularization idea: overfitting happens because the model puts too much weight on irrelevant (usually heavy polynomial) features, so an extra term lambda/(2m) sum theta_j^2 is added to the loss to keep the theta values small. If lambda = 0 there is no regularization; if lambda is very large all theta are driven to 0. The sum starts at j = 1 because theta0 (the intercept) is never penalized, L2 is the squared euclidean norm of theta, and it is vectorized as theta' . theta' with theta'0 = 0.

Exercises 02 and 03 give the regularized loss functions: the regularized linear loss J(theta) = 1/(2m)[(y_hat - y).(y_hat - y) + lambda(theta' . theta')], and the regularized logistic (cross-entropy) loss which adds lambda/(2m)(theta' . theta'); decorators are suggested as a clean implementation.

Exercises 04 and 05 give the regularized gradient: grad(J)0 is unchanged, grad(J)j adds lambda theta_j for j >= 1, and the vectorized form is grad(J) = 1/m [X'^T (h_theta(X) - y) + lambda theta']; the only difference between the linear and logistic versions is h_theta(X) = X' theta versus sigmoid(X' theta).

Exercises 06 to 09 apply everything: the MyRidge class (get_params_, set_params_, loss_, loss_elem_, predict_, gradient_, fit_) is linear regression plus L2, mirrors sklearn.linear_model.Ridge and can inherit from MyLinearRegression; MyLogisticRegression gains a penalty parameter ('l2' or 'none') and a lambda_. Exercise 08 practices regularized logistic regression (polynomial degree 3, several lambda values from 0 to 1, one-vs-all) on solar_system_census, choosing the best model by F1 score on a cross-validation set; exercise 09 practices Ridge regression on space_avocado with a train / cross-validation / test split and lambda from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.2. Libft is the first 42 Common Core project: you build your own static C library (libft.a) by re-implementing a set of standard libc functions plus extra string, memory and singly-linked-list helpers, so you can reuse them in every later C assignment of the cursus.

Libft ("Your very first own library", subject version 19.3) asks you to code a static C library named libft.a, submitted with a Makefile, libft.h and ft_*.c source files. Everything is written in C and must respect the 42 Norm (a norm error anywhere, bonus files included, gives 0), must never crash (segfault, bus error, double free) on defined behaviour, and must free all heap memory with no leaks. The Makefile must provide the rules $(NAME), all, clean, fclean and re, must not relink needlessly, and compiles every .c with cc and the flags -Wall -Wextra -Werror. The archive is built with the ar command; libtool is strictly forbidden, global variables are strictly forbidden, helper functions must be static, all files sit at the repository root, and unused files must not be submitted.

Part 1 re-implements libc functions with the exact prototypes and behaviour of their man pages, only the name changes with an ft_ prefix (strlen becomes ft_strlen). The list: ft_isalpha, ft_isdigit, ft_isalnum, ft_isascii, ft_isprint (returning 1 or 0), ft_strlen, ft_memset, ft_bzero, ft_memcpy, ft_memmove, ft_strlcpy, ft_strlcat, ft_toupper, ft_tolower, ft_strchr, ft_strrchr, ft_strncmp, ft_memchr, ft_memcmp, ft_strnstr, ft_atoi, and — using malloc — ft_calloc and ft_strdup. The restrict qualifier must not appear in your prototypes and the -std=c99 flag must not be used; ft_calloc must return a unique freeable pointer when nmemb or size is 0.

Part 2 adds functions that are not in libc or exist in a different form: ft_substr (a substring from a start index with a maximum length), ft_strjoin (concatenate two strings), ft_strtrim (strip a set of characters from both ends of a string), ft_split (split a string on a delimiter char into a NULL-terminated array of individually allocated strings), ft_itoa (convert an int, negatives included, to a string), ft_strmapi and ft_striteri (apply a function receiving the index and the character, striteri passing the char by address), and the file-descriptor writers ft_putchar_fd, ft_putstr_fd, ft_putendl_fd and ft_putnbr_fd. Every allocating function returns NULL on allocation failure.

Part 3 manipulates a singly linked list through the structure typedef struct s_list { void *content; struct s_list *next; } t_list; declared in libft.h. The functions are ft_lstnew (make a node from a content pointer, next set to NULL), ft_lstadd_front (prepend a node), ft_lstsize (count the nodes), ft_lstlast (return the last node), ft_lstadd_back (append a node), ft_lstdelone (free one node's content with a del function, not the next node), ft_lstclear (free and delete a node and all its successors then set the pointer to NULL), ft_lstiter (apply f to every node's content) and ft_lstmap (build a new list by applying f to each content, using del to free on failure). In this subject version the linked-list part is part of the mandatory part, not a bonus.

A README.md is required at the repository root: its first line italicised as "This project has been created as part of the 42 curriculum by <login>", plus Description, Instructions and Resources sections (the Resources section must state how AI was used, for which tasks and which parts), and a detailed description of the library. The AI Instructions chapter stresses building foundations without shortcuts, not asking the AI for direct answers, and leaning on peer learning because AI is unavailable during exams. During peer-evaluation a brief live modification of the project may be requested to check real understanding; only the git repository is graded, and Deepthought grades after the peer evaluations.

Get Next Line is a 42 Common Core project where you write a function, get_next_line, that returns the next line read from a file descriptor on each successive call, and its main teaching point is the use of static variables in C.

Get Next Line ("Reading a line from a file descriptor is way too tedious", subject version 14.3) has you implement char *get_next_line(int fd); it returns the line read from fd including the terminating \n (except at end of file when the file has no final newline), and returns NULL when there is nothing left to read or on error. Repeated calls in a loop must let you read a text file one line at a time; it must also work when reading from standard input. Allowed external functions are read, malloc and free. The header get_next_line.h must at least contain the prototype, and every helper goes in get_next_line_utils.c; both files plus the header sit at the repository root.

The buffer size for read() is fixed at compile time with the -D BUFFER_SIZE=n option, e.g. cc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -D BUFFER_SIZE=42 *.c; peer evaluators and the Moulinette change that value to test the code, which must compile with and without the flag. The function must still work for a BUFFER_SIZE of 1, 9999 or 10000000. You should read as little as possible per call: as soon as a newline is found, return the current line — do not read the whole file first. Behaviour is undefined if the file is modified between calls before read() reaches EOF, and undefined on binary files (you may still handle that logically).

Forbidden in Get Next Line: using your libft, the lseek() function, and global variables. Common Instructions apply: C only, 42 Norm (norm error including in bonus files gives 0), no unexpected crash on defined behaviour, no memory leaks, a Makefile with $(NAME), all, clean, fclean and re that does not relink, only the git repository is graded, Deepthought grades after peer-evaluation.

The bonus part (assessed only if the mandatory part is perfect) requires get_next_line to use a single static variable and to manage several file descriptors at the same time without mixing up their reading state — reading alternately from fd 3, 4, 5, 3, 4... keeps each descriptor's position. The bonus files carry the _bonus suffix: get_next_line_bonus.c, get_next_line_bonus.h and get_next_line_utils_bonus.c. A README.md is required, including a detailed explanation and justification of the chosen algorithm; the Resources section must describe how AI was used. Once passed, you may add get_next_line to your libft.

Born2beRoot is a 42 Common Core system-administration project: you set up and harden a headless Linux server in a virtual machine (VirtualBox or UTM), with encrypted LVM partitions, SSH, a firewall, a strict password and sudo policy, and a monitoring script.

Born2beRoot (subject version 5.2) introduces virtualization: you build your first VM in VirtualBox (or UTM if VirtualBox is unavailable) and configure the OS under strict rules. The only files submitted are a signature.txt at the repository root holding the SHA1 signature of the VM's virtual disk (.vdi, or .qcow2 for UTM) and the required README.md; the VM itself must never be committed. No snapshots may exist at the start of an evaluation. Starting the VM changes its disk signature, so duplicate the disk or use per-evaluation snapshots; a mismatch between signature.txt and the running VM at defense means a grade of 0.

The OS must be the latest stable Debian (no testing/unstable) or the latest stable Rocky — Debian is recommended for newcomers. No graphical server: installing X.org, Wayland or any equivalent gives 0. For Rocky, KDump is not required but SELinux must run at boot and be configured for the project; for Debian, AppArmor must run at boot. At least 2 encrypted partitions must be created using LVM. At the defense you must explain your OS and know, for example, the difference between aptitude and apt, and what SELinux / AppArmor do.

Networking and access: an SSH service must listen on port 4242 and must refuse root login; SSH is tested at defense by creating a new account. The firewall is UFW (Debian) or firewalld (Rocky), active at boot, with only port 4242 open. The hostname must be your login followed by 42 (e.g. wil42) and you must be able to change it during the review. Besides root, a user named after your login must exist and belong to the user42 and sudo groups; creating a user and adding it to a group is tested at review.

Password policy: passwords expire every 30 days, minimum 2 days between changes, a 7-day expiry warning, at least 10 characters including one uppercase, one lowercase and one digit, no more than 3 consecutive identical characters, must not contain the username, and (root excepted) must differ from the previous password by at least 7 characters; all account passwords including root must then be reset. Sudo policy: authentication limited to 3 attempts, a custom message on a wrong password, every sudo action logged with input and output under /var/log/sudo/, TTY mode enabled, and a restricted secure_path (e.g. /usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/snap/bin).

A bash script monitoring.sh must broadcast to all terminals at boot and every 10 minutes (using wall, driven by cron; you must be able to stop it without modifying it), with no errors displayed. It shows: OS architecture and kernel version, number of physical CPUs, number of virtual CPUs (vCPU), available RAM and its usage percentage, available storage and its usage percentage, current CPU load percentage, date of the last reboot, whether LVM is active, number of active (established TCP) connections, number of logged-in users, the server's IPv4 and MAC address, and the number of commands run with sudo. The bonus part (only if the mandatory part is perfect) asks for a specific partitioning scheme, a working WordPress site served by lighttpd + MariaDB + PHP, and one extra useful service of your choice (NGINX and Apache2 excluded) to justify at defense. The README.md must justify the OS choice and compare Debian vs Rocky, AppArmor vs SELinux, UFW vs firewalld, and VirtualBox vs UTM.

Push_swap is a 42 Common Core algorithm project: sort a stack of unique integers into ascending order using only two stacks and a restricted instruction set, producing the shortest possible sequence of operations.

Push_swap ("Because Swap_push doesn't feel as natural", subject version 10.1) gives you two stacks named a and b and a fixed instruction set; stack a starts with a random number of unique positive and/or negative integers and stack b is empty. You write a C program push_swap that takes stack a as a list of integers (first argument = top of the stack) and prints to standard output the shortest instruction list that sorts a in ascending order with the smallest number at the top, instructions separated only by '\n'. It is the student's first real encounter with algorithmic complexity: sorting is easy, sorting with the fewest moves is the hard part.

The eleven operations are: sa (swap the top two of a), sb (swap the top two of b), ss (sa and sb together), pa (push b's top onto a), pb (push a's top onto b), ra (rotate a up — first element becomes last), rb (rotate b up), rr (ra and rb together), rra (reverse rotate a down — last element becomes first), rrb (reverse rotate b), and rrr (rra and rrb together). Operations that make no sense (swap/push on a too-small or empty stack) simply do nothing.

Rules for the push_swap program (files: Makefile, *.h, *.c; Makefile rules $(NAME), all, clean, fclean, re, no relink): allowed functions are read, write, malloc, free, exit and ft_printf or an equivalent you coded; libft is authorised; global variables are forbidden. With no arguments the program prints nothing and returns to the prompt. On error — a non-integer argument, a value outside int range, or a duplicate — it prints "Error" followed by '\n' on standard error. A displayed list that is too long, or numbers left unsorted, means a grade of 0.

Grading uses a provided binary (checker_OS from the project's intranet resources): ARG="4 67 3 87 23"; ./push_swap $ARG | wc -l counts the moves, and ./push_swap $ARG | ./checker_OS $ARG prints OK or KO. Benchmark: for 100% and bonus eligibility, sort 100 random numbers in fewer than 700 operations and 500 in no more than 5500; minimal validation (grade at least 80%) accepts weaker averages such as 100 in under 1100 and 500 in under 8500. A README.md is required, including how AI was used in the Resources section.

The bonus part (only assessed if the mandatory part is perfect, meaning every benchmark validated) is a second program, checker (files *.h, *.c; Makefile bonus rule; same allowed functions). checker takes stack a as arguments, reads operations from standard input one per line, executes them on the stack, then prints "OK" if a is sorted and b empty, "KO" otherwise, and "Error" on standard error for bad input (non-integer, overflow, duplicate, unknown or malformed instruction). It need not match the provided binary exactly; error handling is mandatory but the parsing style is up to you.

Minitalk is a 42 Common Core project: code a small client/server data-exchange program in C where the client transmits a string to the server one bit at a time using only the UNIX signals SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2.

Minitalk (subject version 5.0) asks for two executables, client and server. The server is started first and prints its PID on launch. The client takes two arguments — the server's PID and the string to send — and transmits that string to the server, which then prints it. Communication must use UNIX signals exclusively, and only SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2 are allowed (typically one signal per bit, 0 or 1). Display must be immediate: if printing 100 characters takes a second the program is too slow. The server must accept strings from several clients in a row without being restarted. Linux does not queue signals when one of that type is already pending, so timing and acknowledgement matter.

Rules: files client and server, a Makefile that does not relink (rules $(NAME), all, clean, fclean, re); libft is authorised; errors must be handled thoroughly and the program must never crash (segfault, bus error, double free) or leak memory. Exactly one global variable per program is allowed (one in the client, one in the server) and its use must be justified. Allowed functions for the mandatory part: write, ft_printf or an equivalent you coded, signal, sigemptyset, sigaddset, sigaction, kill, getpid, malloc, free, pause, sleep, usleep and exit.

The bonus part (assessed only if the mandatory part is perfect) asks the server to acknowledge every received message by sending a signal back to the client, and to support Unicode characters. Pipex is a 42 Common Core project: write a C program that reproduces the shell pipeline < file1 cmd1 | cmd2 > file2, exploring pipes, process creation and file-descriptor redirection.

Pipex (subject version 5.0) is run as ./pipex file1 cmd1 cmd2 file2 and must behave exactly like the shell command < file1 cmd1 | cmd2 > file2 : file1 and file2 are file names, cmd1 and cmd2 are shell commands with their arguments. The program creates a pipe, forks a child per command, redirects standard input/output with dup2, and runs each command with execve after resolving it against the PATH environment variable.

Philosophers is a 42 Common Core concurrency project: implement the dining philosophers problem with threads and mutexes (mandatory) or processes and semaphores (bonus), keeping every philosopher fed while avoiding data races and deadlocks.

Philosophers (subject version 13.0) teaches the basics of threading a process, thread creation and mutexes. The setup: one or more philosophers at a round table with a big bowl of spaghetti; each philosopher alternates eating, thinking and sleeping and never does two at once; there are as many forks as philosophers and a philosopher must hold the fork on their left and the fork on their right to eat, then puts both back and sleeps, then thinks. Philosophers do not communicate and do not know when another is about to die; the simulation ends when a philosopher starves (or, optionally, when every philosopher has eaten enough times).

Global rules (mandatory and bonus): global variables are forbidden; the program takes number_of_philosophers time_to_die time_to_eat time_to_sleep [number_of_times_each_philosopher_must_eat]; times are in milliseconds; a philosopher dies if time_to_die ms pass since the start of their last meal (or the simulation start) without starting to eat; philosophers are numbered 1..N with philosopher 1 next to philosopher N. Every state change is logged as "timestamp_in_ms X has taken a fork", "X is eating", "X is sleeping", "X is thinking" or "X died"; messages must not overlap, a death must be printed within 10 ms of happening, and the program must have no data races.

Mandatory part (program philo, files Makefile, *.h, *.c in philo/; libft NOT authorised): each philosopher is a separate thread, there is one fork between each pair of philosophers (a lone philosopher has only one fork), and each fork's state is protected by a mutex. Allowed functions: memset, printf, malloc, free, write, usleep, gettimeofday, pthread_create, pthread_detach, pthread_join, pthread_mutex_init, pthread_mutex_destroy, pthread_mutex_lock, pthread_mutex_unlock.

Bonus part (program philo_bonus, files in philo_bonus/; assessed only if the mandatory part is perfect): same arguments and global rules, but each philosopher is a separate process (the main process is not a philosopher), all forks sit in the middle of the table with no in-memory state, and the number of available forks is represented by a semaphore. Extra allowed functions: fork, kill, exit, waitpid, sem_open, sem_close, sem_post, sem_wait, sem_unlink. Parsing and quoting: unclosed quotes and un-required special characters such as backslash (\) and semicolon (;) do not have to be interpreted; single quotes ' prevent interpretation of every metacharacter in the quoted sequence; double quotes " prevent interpretation of every metacharacter except the dollar sign $. Redirections and pipes: < redirects input, > redirects output, >> redirects output in append mode, and << reads input until a line matching a given delimiter (heredoc — it does not have to update history). Pipes (|) connect each command's output to the next command's input. Signals must behave like bash in interactive mode: ctrl-C prints a new prompt on a new line, ctrl-D exits the shell, ctrl-\ does nothing. The built-ins to implement are echo (with -n), cd (relative or absolute path only), pwd (no options), export (no options), unset (no options), env (no options or arguments) and exit (no options). readline may leak memory (you need not fix that) but your own code must not leak. The bonus part (evaluated only if the mandatory part is perfect) adds && and || with parentheses for priority, and wildcards * working for the current working directory. miniRT is a 42 Common Core computer-graphics project: write a basic ray tracer in C with MiniLibX that renders a scene of simple geometric primitives (plane, sphere, cylinder) with ambient and diffuse lighting, from a .rt scene description file.

miniRT ("My first RayTracer with MiniLibX", subject version 10.0) contrasts ray tracing (developed in 1968, computationally expensive, very realistic) with rasterization; its stated goal is to prove you can implement any mathematical or physical formula without being a mathematician. Files: all your files, a Makefile with rules all, clean, fclean, re and bonus; libft is authorised. Allowed functions: open, close, read, write, printf, malloc, free, perror, strerror, exit, gettimeofday, every math library function (-lm) and every MiniLibX function. Window management must stay fluid, ESC and the window's red close cross quit cleanly, and using MiniLibX images is recommended.

Rendering requirements: at least the three primitives plane, sphere and cylinder, with all intersections and object insides handled correctly; you must be able to resize each object's unique property (sphere diameter, cylinder diameter and height); translation and rotation transforms apply to objects, lights and cameras (spheres and lights cannot be rotated); lighting must include ambient light (nothing is ever fully dark) and diffuse lighting, plus spot brightness and hard shadows. The scene file is the first argument and has the .rt extension.

The .rt format: elements are separated by line breaks, an element's fields by spaces, elements may be in any order, and elements identified by a capital letter appear only once. Each line starts with a type identifier: A = ambient light (ratio [0.0,1.0] then R,G,B); C = camera (x,y,z position, then a normalized 3D orientation vector, then horizontal FOV in degrees [0,180]); L = light (x,y,z position, brightness ratio [0.0,1.0], then R,G,B — colour unused in the mandatory part); sp = sphere (center x,y,z, diameter, R,G,B); pl = plane (a point x,y,z, a normalized normal vector, R,G,B); cy = cylinder (center x,y,z, normalized axis vector, diameter, height, R,G,B). Any misconfiguration makes the program exit with "Error\n" followed by an explicit message; bring a set of working scenes to the defense.

The bonus part (evaluated only if the mandatory part is perfect and cannot fail even on bad input) may add: specular reflection for a full Phong reflection model, a checkerboard colour pattern, coloured and multi-spot lights, one more second-degree object (cone, hyperboloid, paraboloid), and bump-map textures; extra functions and scene-format changes are allowed if justified. Inception is a 42 Common Core system-administration project: inside a virtual machine, build a small multi-service infrastructure with Docker Compose — NGINX (TLS-only), WordPress + php-fpm, and MariaDB — each in its own container from a hand-written Dockerfile, wired by a docker network and named volumes.

Inception (subject version 5.3) is done in a VM; all config files live in a srcs folder and a Makefile at the repository root builds the whole application via docker-compose.yml. Each service runs in its own dedicated container whose image has the same name as the service; images are built from the penultimate stable Alpine or Debian and from your own Dockerfiles (pulling ready-made images or using DockerHub is forbidden, Alpine/Debian excepted); the latest tag is prohibited. Containers must restart on crash. Forbidden hacks: network: host, --link, links:, and any infinite-loop entrypoint (tail -f, bash, sleep infinity, while true) — read about PID 1 and Dockerfile best practices; the network line must be in docker-compose.yml.

Required services and storage: an NGINX container as the single entrypoint on port 443 only, with TLSv1.2 or TLSv1.3 only; a WordPress + php-fpm container with no nginx; a MariaDB container with no nginx; one named volume for the WordPress database and one for the website files, both stored under /home/login/data on the host (bind mounts forbidden for these); a docker network connecting the containers. The WordPress database has two users, one being the administrator whose name must not contain admin/administrator in any form. The domain login.42.fr must point to the local IP. No password may appear in a Dockerfile — use environment variables and a .env file, Docker secrets are strongly recommended; any credential committed to git (outside proper secrets) fails the project.

Directory layout: Makefile and secrets/ (credentials.txt, db_password.txt, db_root_password.txt) at the root, srcs/ containing docker-compose.yml, .env and requirements/ with one folder per service (mariadb, nginx, wordpress, tools, bonus), each with its Dockerfile and conf/. The README.md (in English) must explain the Docker usage and compare Virtual Machines vs Docker, Secrets vs Environment Variables, Docker Network vs Host Network, and Docker Volumes vs Bind Mounts; USER_DOC.md and DEV_DOC.md are also required. The bonus part (only if the mandatory part is perfect) adds a Redis cache for WordPress, an FTP server on the website volume, a static non-PHP website, Adminer, and one extra useful service, each with its own Dockerfile.

ft_irc is a 42 Common Core network-programming project: write your own IRC server in C++98 (ircserv), reachable by a real IRC client, handling many clients at once over TCP/IP with a single non-blocking poll() loop, with authentication, channels, private messages and channel-operator commands.

ft_irc (subject version 11.0) requires a program ircserv run as ./ircserv <port> <password>: the port it listens on and the password every client must provide. You must not write an IRC client and must not implement server-to-server communication. C++98 rules apply: c++ -Wall -Wextra -Werror, compiles with -std=c++98, a non-relinking Makefile with $(NAME), all, clean, fclean, re, no external or Boost libraries, prefer C++ headers (<cstring> over <string.h>). The server must never crash or quit unexpectedly (grade 0 otherwise). Allowed system calls include socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv, setsockopt, getaddrinfo, htons/ntohs, poll (or select/kqueue/epoll), signal/sigaction, fcntl, close, lseek, fstat.

Concurrency requirements: handle multiple clients simultaneously without hanging; forking is prohibited; all I/O must be non-blocking; exactly one poll() (or equivalent) handles every operation — read, write, listen — and you must never read/recv or write/send on any fd without going through poll() (grade 0), nor rely on errno (e.g. EAGAIN) to decide what to do next (grade 0). On macOS, fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK) is allowed (only that flag). Communication is TCP/IP v4 or v6. You pick one real IRC client as the reference for the defense; it must connect without error. Because TCP delivers data in pieces, you must aggregate received packets to rebuild each command (test with nc -C sending 'com', 'man', 'd').

Features to implement (only these): authenticate with the password, set a nickname and a username, join a channel, send and receive private messages; every message a client sends to a channel is forwarded to all other members; there are operators and regular users. Channel-operator commands: KICK (eject a client), INVITE (invite a client), TOPIC (view or change the channel topic), and MODE with the flags i (invite-only), t (restrict TOPIC to operators), k (channel key/password), o (grant/revoke operator), l (user limit). The README.md is in English. The bonus part (only if the mandatory part is perfect) adds file transfer and a bot.

Webserv is a 42 Common Core network project: write your own HTTP/1.1 server in C++98 (webserv), configured by an NGINX-style config file, testable with a real browser, serving static sites, handling file uploads and CGI, all on a single non-blocking poll() loop.

Webserv (subject version 24.1) requires a program webserv run as ./webserv [configuration file] (a default path is used if omitted). C++98 rules apply: c++ -Wall -Wextra -Werror, compiles with -std=c++98, a non-relinking Makefile with $(NAME), all, clean, fclean, re, no external or Boost libraries, prefer C++ headers. The server must never crash or terminate unexpectedly (grade 0). It may not execve another web server. Allowed functions include socket, bind, listen, accept, send, recv, select/poll/epoll/kqueue, fcntl, dup2, fork, execve, pipe, waitpid, stat, open, opendir/readdir/closedir, chdir, and more. Read the HTTP RFCs and test with telnet and NGINX; HTTP/1.0 is a suggested reference point, not enforced.

I/O requirements: the server stays non-blocking at all times; exactly one poll() (or equivalent) drives all client/server I/O including listen, and it must watch reading and writing simultaneously; you must never read or write without going through poll(), and checking errno after a read/write to adjust behaviour is strictly forbidden (grade 0) — regular disk files are exempt from the poll requirement. A request must never hang indefinitely; response status codes must be accurate; the server must ship default error pages; fork is only allowed for CGI; it must serve a fully static website, allow file uploads, implement at least GET, POST and DELETE, listen on multiple ports, and survive a stress test. On macOS, fcntl is allowed only with F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK and FD_CLOEXEC.

The configuration file (inspired by an NGINX server block) lets you set: the interface:port pairs to listen on (multiple servers), default error pages, the maximum client request body size, and per-route (location) rules without regex — accepted HTTP methods, HTTP redirection, the root directory for the URL (e.g. /kapouet rooted to /tmp/www maps /kapouet/pouic/toto/pouet to /tmp/www/pouic/toto/pouet), directory listing on/off, a default file for directory requests, an upload directory, and CGI execution by file extension (e.g. .php). For CGI: pass the full request via environment variables, un-chunk chunked requests (the CGI expects EOF as end of body), treat EOF as end of CGI output when there is no Content-Length, and run the CGI in the right directory. The README.md is in English. The bonus part (only if the mandatory part is perfect) adds cookies/session management and multiple CGI types.

web application team project with modules

ft_transcendence is the final 42 Common Core project: a team of 4-5 people builds a real-world web application (frontend + backend + database, containerized) of their own design, then earns at least 14 points by implementing chosen Major (2 pts) and Minor (1 pt) modules.

ft_transcendence (subject version 21.1) is a group project (4-5 people) with defined team roles — Product Owner, Project Manager / Scrum Master, Technical Lead / Architect, and Developers (everyone) — all documented in the README.md, and the team is questioned at evaluation on how roles, work and communication were organised. It has a fixed mandatory core every member contributes to, plus modules that count toward the grade. Project ideas are open (a multiplayer Pong with tournaments, a social network, an online Chess/Tic-Tac-Toe with matchmaking, a collaborative platform, etc.) but must satisfy the constraints.

General requirements (failing any = rejection): it must be a web application with a frontend, a backend and a database; Git with meaningful commits from all members and clear work distribution; deployment via a containerization solution (Docker/Podman/equivalent) with a single command; compatible with the latest stable Google Chrome; no browser-console warnings or errors; accessible non-placeholder Privacy Policy and Terms of Service pages (footer links); and multi-user support — several users logged in and acting concurrently with no data corruption or race conditions.

Technical requirements: a clear, responsive, accessible frontend using a CSS framework/solution of choice; credentials in a git-ignored .env with an .env.example; a database with a clear schema and relations; a basic user management system with secure sign-up/login (at least email + password, hashed and salted); frontend and backend input validation; and HTTPS for every connection to the backend from a browser/script/API (internal backend traffic may be unencrypted). The subject defines what counts as a framework (React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, Express, Fastify, NestJS, Django, Flask... — not jQuery/Lodash/Axios).

Modules: you need 14 points total, Major = 2 points, Minor = 1 point, across categories Web, Accessibility & Internationalization, User Management, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Gaming & user experience, DevOps, Data & Analytics, Blockchain, and Modules of choice. Examples: use a frontend + backend framework, real-time WebSockets, a public API with 5+ endpoints, an ORM, OAuth 2.0, 2FA, a web-based game, remote players, a tournament system, an AI opponent, a full RAG or LLM system, WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility, 3+ languages i18n, ELK log management, Prometheus + Grafana monitoring, microservices, blockchain tournament scores on Avalanche/Solidity. Some modules depend on others (gaming modules require a game first; SSR is incompatible with the ICP blockchain backend). Only fully functional modules score; the README.md (in English) must detail team roles, project management, technical stack, database schema, features, modules with point calculation and justification, and individual contributions. The bonus part (only after the 14 mandatory points) counts extra modules for up to 5 more points.
